idiom_name: SDK or HTTP-client retry (auto keys, ky/undici) + crypto.randomUUID()
implementation_notes: The retry loop normally comes from a client library, and the best of them also own the key: Stripe's server SDKs add an idempotency key to every request automatically once network retries are enabled, which is the pattern delivered as a library contract, while the popular JavaScript HTTP clients (ky, axios-retry, undici's RetryHandler) replay requests and leave key management to the caller. When you write it yourself the platform still supplies the primitive - crypto.randomUUID() on the web and in Node, node:crypto's randomUUID - and the wrapper must capture the key outside the retry, put it in the request headers and reuse that exact request description. There is no classic object structure to replace here; the failure mode is not a missing framework but a key minted in the wrong scope.
pitfalls: Regenerating the key inside the retry callback (or inside a fetch interceptor) is the standard bug: every attempt becomes a new operation and the server has nothing to deduplicate on.

Automatic retries are frequently on by default in SDKs and proxies; enabling network retries without keys guarantees duplicates for POSTs, and a Request/AbortSignal that was already consumed cannot be replayed at all.
crypto.randomUUID() requires a secure context in browsers, so on plain http:// pages it is undefined; feature-detect it and fall back to a CSPRNG-derived id rather than Math.random().
